name: Mange

agents.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
agents.notes: A burrowing mite that excavates tunnels in the epidermis and causes intense pruritus. It is highly contagious and can affect humans — the human form is classical scabies, and animal-derived infections cause a self-limiting but intensely itchy dermatitis.
agents.reservoir: Infested animals; the mite does not survive long off the host

agents.name: Psoroptes ovis
agents.notes: A non-burrowing, surface-living mite that feeds on epidermal debris and causes a severe exudative dermatitis with thick scabs. It is the cause of sheep scab, a serious welfare and economic disease in sheep.
agents.reservoir: Infested sheep; the mite can survive on fences and handling equipment for a short period

agents.name: Chorioptes bovis
agents.notes: A surface mite that typically affects the lower limbs and tail of cattle, causing less severe disease than Sarcoptes or Psoroptes. Often associated with 'leg mange' and tail-head dermatitis.

hosts.notes: Each mite species has a preferred host but can often infest related species. Sheep are the most commonly affected livestock species in terms of welfare impact. Goats are highly susceptible to Sarcoptes.

notifiable.note: Psoroptic mange in sheep (sheep scab) is subject to statutory control in several countries and has been a notifiable disease in some jurisdictions. It is not currently WOAH-listed.

distribution: Worldwide. Mange is a disease of crowding, poor body condition and limited access to veterinary care. In southern Africa, sarcoptic and psoroptic mange are economically significant in sheep, goats and cattle, particularly in communal and extensively managed flocks.

aetiology.summary: Mange is transmitted by direct contact between animals, with mites surviving only briefly off the host. The disease is therefore a function of stocking density, mixing and the immune and nutritional status of the animals. Outbreaks in well-managed herds are usually traceable to an introduced infested animal.
determinants: Direct contact with an infested animal
Mite survival on fomites such as fences, crushes and bedding for short periods
Crowding and mixing of animals from different sources
Compromised immunity and poor body condition
Absence of a treatment or control programme in an affected group
risk_factors: Overcrowding in pens, kraals or transport
Introducing untested or untreatably infested animals into a clean herd
Poor nutrition and concurrent disease, which increase susceptibility and severity
Shearing and handling equipment that is not cleaned between flocks
aetiology.epidemiology: The mites have a direct life cycle completed entirely on the host, with a generation time of 2-3 weeks. Transmission requires close contact, so the disease spreads slowly through a herd unless animals are crowded. Sarcoptic mange is more contagious and more pruritic than chorioptic mange, which tends to be chronic and localised to the legs and tail.

pathophysiology.summary: The mite's feeding and burrowing damage the epidermis and provoke an intense hypersensitivity reaction to mite antigens and faeces. The resultant pruritus drives self-trauma, and the combination of excoriation, secondary bacterial infection and serum exudation produces the thickened, crusted skin that characterises the disease.

cascade.title: Mite establishment
cascade.detail: Mites transfer from an infested animal and establish on the new host. Sarcoptes burrows into the stratum corneum; Psoroptes and Chorioptes remain on the surface and feed on epidermal debris and tissue fluid.

cascade.title: Sensitisation
cascade.detail: After an initial period of 2-3 weeks, the host becomes sensitised to mite antigens and develops an intense type I and type IV hypersensitivity reaction, which is responsible for most of the pruritus.

cascade.title: Self-trauma and excoriation
cascade.detail: Intense itching causes rubbing, biting and scratching, which excoriates the skin, damages hair follicles and creates secondary lesions that spread beyond the original sites of mite activity.

cascade.title: Epidermal hyperplasia and crusting
cascade.detail: Chronic irritation produces hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and a thickened, folded appearance to the skin with adherent crusts, alopecia and lichenification.

cascade.title: Secondary infection and debility
cascade.detail: Bacterial infection of excoriated skin is common. In severe and prolonged cases, chronic pruritus, loss of condition and reduced feed intake produce significant debility and can contribute to mortality, particularly in young or malnourished animals.

lesions: Papules, vesicles and crusts on the face, ears, neck and flanks in sarcoptic mange
Thick, adherent, yellowish scabs over large areas of the body in psoroptic mange
Alopecia, lichenification and thickened, folded skin in chronic cases
Excoriation and secondary pyoderma from self-trauma
Chorioptic mange: lesions on the lower limbs, tail and perineum
Emaciation and poor body condition in severe cases
clinical_signs: Intense pruritus, with persistent rubbing, biting and scratching
Hair loss, starting on the face, ears and neck in sarcoptic mange
Thick scabs and crusts, often with a musty odour
Thickened, corrugated skin in chronic cases
Restlessness and reduced grazing, leading to weight loss
Rubbing against fences and posts to the point of excoriation
Secondary bacterial infection with pustules and exudate

antemortem: Skin scraping from the margin of a fresh lesion — ideally several sites, because mites can be hard to find
Examine the scrapings microscopically; Sarcoptes is best recovered from deep scrapings of the most recent lesions
Consider a therapeutic trial when mites are not found but the clinical picture is compatible
postmortem: Mange is diagnosed on the live animal; post-mortem findings are limited to skin lesions and secondary infection
Note emaciation and the distribution of skin lesions
laboratory: Microscopic examination of skin scrapings for mites or eggs
ELISA for Sarcoptes antibodies, available in some countries for herd screening
PCR-based identification of species from skin lesions, increasingly used for confirmation
Histopathology of skin biopsy, which shows eosinophilic dermatitis with mites in some cases
differentials: Dermatophilosis — paintbrush scabs and a wet-environment association, different organisms on smear
Ringworm — circular lesions with raised margins and hair loss, fungal elements on microscopy
Photosensitisation — dermatitis restricted to unpigmented skin, no mites
Zinc deficiency — crusting on the face and limbs with a nutritional history
Allergic dermatitis from insects or plant contact
Poxvirus skin lesions, such as lumpy skin disease

prevention: Quarantine and treat all incoming animals before mixing with the herd
Avoid overcrowding and reduce stocking density in pens and kraals
Maintain adequate nutrition, as poor body condition increases susceptibility
Clean and disinfect handling equipment, rails and shared rubbing posts
Monitor herds regularly and treat early when pruritus is noticed
control.vaccination: No vaccine is available. Control relies on acaricide treatment and management.
treatment: Macrocyclic lactones, particularly ivermectin and doramectin, are the most effective and widely used treatment
Moxidectin and eprinomectin are alternatives with variable residual activity
Organophosphate or amitraz dips are used in some countries but resistance and residue concerns limit their use
Treat the entire affected group rather than individual animals, because in-contact animals are often infested subclinically
Repeat treatment at intervals matching the mite life cycle — usually two treatments 10-14 days apart
outbreak: Treat all animals in the affected group simultaneously
Repeat treatment to catch newly hatched mites
Isolate and treat affected animals where practical
Clean and disinfect equipment and shared rubbing surfaces
Trace the source — usually an introduced animal — and review biosecurity
Notify the veterinary authority where statutory control applies, notably for sheep scab
public_health: Animal-derived Sarcoptes can cause transient, self-limiting dermatitis in people — an itchy rash on the forearms and hands is common in handlers
Human scabies from the human-adapted mite is a different condition and spreads person-to-person, not from livestock
Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling infested animals, and wash thoroughly afterwards
Animal mites do not establish sustained infestations on humans, so human cases resolve once exposure stops
control.notes: The most common cause of treatment failure is treating only the visibly affected animals. Mites survive at low levels on in-contact animals, and any untreated animal becomes a source of reinfestation.

prognosis: Good with appropriate treatment of the whole group and improved management. Chronic cases with extensive skin damage take weeks to recover. Welfare implications are significant in untreated animals, and chronic cases can contribute to mortality in already debilitated stock.
